newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish army targets Islamist grip on power.
newsitem.headline: Turkish army targets Islamist grip on power.

text.p: Turkey's powerful armed forces have rattled their secularist sabres ahead of a key government meeting at the weekend, sending civilian politicians of all stripes running for cover.
Investors were not far behind, dumping shares on the Istanbul Stock Exchange and sending the main index down almost seven percent at midday on Thursday.

Tough remarks aimed at Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan from a top gendarme commander -- backed up by other senor officers -- shattered the calm of the Moslem Feast of the Sacrifice earlier this week.

The reverberations from a military establishment that has toppled civilian rule three times in the last four decades exposed the deep fault lines in the coalition between Erbakan's Islamists and the secularists of Tansu Ciller's True Path Party.

They also set the stage for a potential showdown on Saturday, when the military-dominated National Security Council is expected to repeat demands to Erbakan's recalcitrant cabinet for an anti-Islamist crackdown.
"The political picture reveals the government is now finished," said commentator Bilal Cetin.

"The military does not want it, even other institutions do not want it," Cetin told Reuters. The only question, he said, surrounded an immediate way out of the impasse between the Islamists and a secularist establishment led by the generals.
Investors voted with their pocketbooks, sending Istanbul shares down 6.85 percent to 1,427 at the close of morning trade.
"The dominant view (in the market) is that the government will fall," said Korhan Biricik from Deha securities, adding a drop to around 1,350, or another 5.3 percent, was possible by the weekend.

The latest escalation in the armed forces' political war of attrition with the Erbakan-led government began with comments from General Osman Ozbek, head of the gendarmerie in the eastern province of Erzurum.
Ozbek denounced Erbakan as a pimp for accepting the hospitality of Saudi Arabia's conservative king during his haj pilgrimage to Mecca this month.
"If he were a real man he wouldn't go as a guest of a king like that...I do not care whether he is prime minister or minister of whatever...the pimp," Ozbek said.
"Some of those making use of democracy are trying to come to power by cutting throats as in Algeria," he said in a reference to radical Islamist violence in the North African country.
His remarks, made at a closed meeting, were leaked to major newspapers and a video tape of his speech was broadcast on many television channels, most controlled by secularist interests.
In what was widely seen as public endorsement for Ozbek, Army Commander Hikmet Koksal refused demands by the ruling Islamist Welfare Party to rein in the soldiers.
"There is no way we can zip anybody's mouth," Koksal told reporters.

Senior politicians from across the spectrum, eager to head off any possibility of direct military intervention, scrambled to paste together a workable government formula to supplant Erbakan's coalition, formed last June.
Main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz floated two variants, each by-passing the party chiefs, whose squabbling has doomed past attempts at a cabinet that would exclude the Islamists.

The proposals, Yilmaz told the daily Hurriyet in comments published on Thursday, were designed to lead the country to early elections in 1998 or 1999. The next scheduled general polls are ostensibly set for December of 2000.
Meanwhile, influential elements of Erbakan's Welfare Party, as well as ministers from Ciller's True Path, are openly talking about scrapping their 10-month-old coalition.

President Suleyman Demirel, himself the victim of two military interventions as prime minister, has also jumped in to suggest that early elections -- which he has the power to call -- might offer the best way out of the current deadlock.
